svg.text: EQUATION 1 — the expected colour of one camera ray
Walk the ray. At every point ask: is light still
travelling, does it stop here, what colour is here?
The pixel is the average colour where it stops.

a.data-tip: The probability that the ray travels from the near bound to t without hitting any other particle. It starts at exactly 1 at the near bound and can only fall, because the integral in its exponent only grows. This is the occlusion term: it is why a wall hides what is behind it, and it is the only part of Equation 1 that looks backwards along the ray.
a.text: accumulated transmittance — the term you cannot guess
T(t) = exp( - ∫ from near to t of σ(r(s)) ds )
The probability the ray survives from the near bound to t un-occluded.
Starts at 1, only ever falls, and mutes everything behind the first opaque thing.

g.data-tiphead: The shape of T along a ray
g.data-tip: Flat and near 1 through empty space, then a cliff at the first opaque surface, then flat and near zero for the rest of the ray.

a.data-tip: The differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at that location. Not a colour and not an opacity by itself: it is a rate, so what a slab of thickness delta actually blocks is 1 minus exp of minus sigma times delta. It is a function of position alone.
a.text: The differential probability of a ray terminating at an
infinitesimal particle there — a rate, not an opacity, and it
depends on position only, never on direction.

a.data-tip: The RGB the point sends back along direction d. Because it takes the direction as an input, the same point can look white to one camera and orange to another, which is how the model reproduces highlights and reflections. There is no light source in the model: the colour is emitted, so the lighting is baked in.
a.text: Takes the viewing direction, so one point can look white
from here and orange from there. No light source exists:
the lighting is baked into the emitted radiance.

svg.text: T(t)·σ(t) is a density over where along the ray the light stops. It integrates to at most 1: the rest is transmitted past the far bound.
Integrate colour against that density and you get the pixel. Slide 17 works it through, including what fills the remainder.
